newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi army seen gaining by Zaire refugee exodus.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army seen gaining by Zaire refugee exodus.

text.p: Burundi's Tutsi army, waging a bitter civil war with Hutu rebels, may gain from the mass flight of Hutu refugees from camps just inside Zaire but chaos there could eventually engulf the small Central African state, analysts say.

Hutu rebels from the Democratic Defence Forces (FDD) have fled camps north of the Zairean town of Uvira along with around 230,000 Burundian and Rwandan refugees because of fighting over the city, which is just across Lake Tanganyika from Bujumbura.
In the short term the collapse of the camps could help Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army, which seized power on July 25, to fight rebels of the Hutu majority.

The international community, through the United Nations, was effectively funding a Burundian rebel army in exile -- as it did further north in Zaire by giving aid to Rwandan Hutu refugees whose teeming camps included 40,000 soldiers of the former government that instigated genocide against Rwanda's Tutsis.

Burundi's Hutu Rebels were largely based in camps near Uvira, security source said, bringing communications equipment and armaments such as machineguns and rocket-propelled grenade launchers from stores into Burundi, using a supply line running from Cibitoke in the northwest across to Tanzania through their main base inside Burundi at Kibira forest. Now that supply line is broken at the Uvira end.

"The Burundian army has one mission at the moment and that is to wipe out the FDD units moving across the country. This is probably a unique opportunity to strike against the FDD's capacity to continue its guerrilla war," a senior diplomat said.

Burundi and Rwanda deny supporting ethnic Tutsi rebels fighting Zairean troops in eastern Zaire around Uvira and Bukavu. Burundi has sealed its border with Zaire, stationing hundreds of extra troops on the frontier to screen refugees coming across.
Privately, military commanders concede the advantage of having a Tutsi buffer zone on Burundi's western border, but they say this is offset by the prospect of an unstable Zaire.

"In the short term of course it could be good for us, but in the medium and long term it cannot be good to have hundreds of thousands of refugees on the move near the western border," army spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi said.
Around 150,000 people have been killed in Burundi since October 1993 when the country's first Hutu president was murdered in an attempted coup by Tutsi soldiers.
"The Hutu-Tutsi conflict is spilling over massively into eastern Zaire and this could fuel a regional war," one senior Burundi government official told Reuters.

Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels, who say they are fighting because of the persecution of an estimated 300,000 Banyamulenge by authorities in Zaire's South Kivu region, have launched attacks in eastern Zaire causing up to half a million refugees to flee.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali this weekend called for a regional summit to address the root causes of ethnic conflict in Rwanda, Burundi and Zaire.
But the call rings hollow according to some African analysts who question who would represent Burundi, a country still deeply divided over the coup staged in July by the Tutsi army.

Burundi's military regime was ostracised by regional neighbours including Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Zaire when they imposed economic sanctions six days after the July coup which brought ethnic Tutsi Pierre Buyoya to power.
Burundi comes before the U.N. Security Council at the end of October when a 60-day deadline for the start of all- party negotiations is due to expire.
Regional leaders should meet in the Zambian capital Lusaka on November 11 to decide on whether Buyoya has done enough to merit a relaxation of sanctions.
Diplomats argue regional states, suddenly faced with a problem greater than Burundi's ethnic conflict, could end up relaxing sanctions.
"Up till now the debate has been focused very closely on Burundi...Now the regional problem has helped to increase pressure for some easing of sanctions," a diplomat said.
"What we could be seeing is the start of the break-up of Zaire," the diplomat added.
